newsitem.title: USA: Japan seeks summit support in islands dispute.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks summit support in islands dispute.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto asked the Group of Seven nations and Russia on Friday night to support efforts for a solution to a long-running territorial dispute with Moscow, a Japanese spokesman said on Friday night.

Hashimoto made the request at a dinner launching the annual G7 summit -- in which Russian President Borin Yeltsin is also taking part -- and pointed out that Tokyo had allowed Russia to participate in the group's discussions.

"Japan has agreed to let Russia formally join the G7 summit...I would like to ask for your cooperation in solving problems which Japan and Russia have to solve," the spokesman quoted Hashimoto as saying.
The prime minister said he and Yeltsin agreed on Friday morning to try to solve the dispute over Russian-held islands.

"The prime minister told the other summit members that Japan accepted the U.S. request to let Russia join the G7 without any hesitation despite problems that Japan and Russia have to solve," the spokesman said.

It was not clear whether Hashimoto was just referring to Yeltsin's participation in the Denver summit or was endorsing his drive for full Russian membership of the rich nations' club. France said before Friday's dinner there was a consensus against Russia joining.

The three-day summit groups leaders of the G7 -- the United States, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan -- with Yeltsin present for all sessions except one on financial and economic policy on Saturday. The meeting has been formally dubbed the "Summit of the Eight".
Japan decided to drop its previous opposition to Russia's participation in the summit fearing its stand could eventually undermine its efforts to win back the islands.

The dispute centres on four Russian-controlled islands and islet groups, called the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kuriles by Russia, that were seized by the Soviet Union in the closing days of the Second World War.

Japan says the islands must be returned. Yeltsin, aware that territorial concessions would prompt a fierce backlash from his nationalist opponents, says there is no question of handing them over to Tokyo.
The dispute has prevented the two countries signing a formal peace treaty ending wartime hostilities.
